2.title: Published Figure 2: learned hedge and model hedge
2.original_caption: Comparison of model hedge and deep hedge associated to $50\%$-expected shortfall criterion.

axes.vertical: Number of simulated outcomes in a bin

2.interpretation_markdown: Blue bars show the $50\%$-CVaR hedge; orange bars show the model hedge. The horizontal axis is terminal profit and loss, $q-L$, using the same premium $q\approx1.69$. Negative values are losses. Bar heights count outcomes. Both distributions concentrate near zero and have similar shapes: in this zero-cost example, the learned hedge behaves much like the model hedge.
2.comparison_note_markdown: Our saved runs use $c=0.001$ and different training and simulation choices. Our stock-delta benchmark trades only stock; the published model hedge also trades the variance claim. Compare distribution shapes and tails while keeping these setup differences explicit. Bar heights also depend on sample counts and bin widths.

11.title: Published Figure 11: trading costs and entropic pricing

setup.numerical_price_reference: Risk-neutral Heston value q; the displayed axis labels the reference p_0.
setup.reference_explanation: Section 5.3 states that the numerical plots compare with q, ignoring the separate discrete-rebalancing premium.

11.interpretation_markdown: Red dots are the authors' results at five trading-cost rates; the blue line is a fitted trend. Moving right means higher costs, and moving up means a larger price premium. The slope $0.71$ describes approximately power-law scaling over this tested range. It concerns the effect of costs. The axis uses $p_0$; Section 5.3 explains that the numerical reference is $q$.
11.comparison_note_markdown: Our saved comparison fixes $c=0.001$, so it does not estimate this cost-scaling slope. This original figure motivates a later cost sweep. Our current graphs compare networks and risk objectives under common settings; their values should not be overlaid as matched replications of these published points.
